rows.description: A toddler pours sand from cup to cup for a long stretch, deaf to calls for lunch. Total absorption in a task of the right size is the earliest form of flow, and being pulled out abruptly can bring tears.

rows.description: A toddler bangs pots, splashes water and drops spoons repeatedly to see what happens. This is not mischief but experimentation, and the repetition is how cause and effect is learned.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child runs a make-believe shop or hospital, assigning roles and correcting others who break the story. Pretend play rehearses adult life, emotions and rules in a safe frame.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: Left without screens on a long summer afternoon, a child builds a fort, invents a game or draws for hours. Tolerated boredom is where self-directed interest first grows.

related mind states: interest, boredom

rows.description: A teenager scrolls compulsively, switching apps to escape a flat feeling. The boredom is less about lack of options and more about intolerance for an empty moment.

rows.description: A student who feels bored in a course asks whether the material is too easy, too hard or simply meaningless to them. Reading boredom as data, not just a nuisance, guides better choices.

rows.description: A child fights bedtime, wanting one more story or fearing missing out. Predictable routines and calm endings teach that rest is safe and does not mean being left out.

rows.description: Adults worry when a quiet child prefers being alone and push them into groups. Checking for real distress is wise, but preference for solitude is often just temperament.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A young professional schedules quiet time without a device, on a terrace or a morning walk. Solitude used deliberately sorts thoughts and sharpens decisions.

rows.description: A teenager moved by a scientist, a mountain, a devotional song or a stranger's kindness feels lifted beyond daily worries. Awe can arise from moral beauty as much as from scenery.
